**Surah al-Mumtahanah (The Examined Woman)**
It has thirteen verses and was revealed at Medina.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, showing them affection,﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, showing them affection,﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Know that the way in which this surah is connected to what came before it is that both address the condition of the Messenger ﷺ together with those present in his time, from the Jews, the Christians and others. Some of them hastened to make peace and acknowledged his truthfulness, and among them were the Banu al-Nadir, for they said: "By Allah, he is the Prophet whose description and attributes we found in the Torah." Others of them denied this and resorted to fighting, either openly or secretly, for they were with the people of Islam outwardly and with the people of disbelief inwardly. As for the connection of the first part with the last part, it is clear, because the end of that surah (al-Mumtahanah's preceding surah, al-Saff) includes the praiseworthy attributes of the Presence of Allah, the Exalted, such as His oneness and others, while the beginning of this surah includes the prohibition of mixing with those who do not acknowledge those attributes.

**The second issue:** As for the occasion of revelation, it has been narrated that it was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, when he wrote to the people of Makkah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was preparing for the conquest and intended to attack them, so take your precautions. Then he sent that letter with a woman, a freedwoman of the Banu Hashim, called Sarrah, who came to the Prophet ﷺ from Makkah to Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, said: "Have you come as a Muslim?" She said: "No." He said: "Have you come as an emigrant?" She said: "No." He said: "Then what has brought you?" She said: "The clients (mawali) have perished on the Day of Badr," meaning they were killed on that day, "and I am in dire need." So he urged the Banu al-Muttalib to help her, and they clothed her, provided her with a mount and provisions. Then Hatib came to her, gave her ten dinars and clothed her with a cloak, and asked her to carry that letter to the people of Makkah. She set off, but Allah informed the Messenger, peace be upon him, of this. So he sent Ali, Umar, Ammar, Talhah and al-Zubayr after her, and they were horsemen. They overtook her and asked her about it, but she denied it and swore. Ali, peace be upon him, said: "By Allah, we have not lied, nor has the Messenger of Allah lied," and he drew his sword. So she brought the letter out from the braids of her hair. They brought the letter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he showed it to Hatib, who confessed. He said: "I have a family and property in Makkah, and I wanted to draw close to them. I knew that Allah, the Exalted, would send down His punishment upon them." He (the Prophet) accepted his truthfulness and his excuse. Umar said: "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "What do you know, O Umar? Perhaps Allah, the Exalted, has looked upon the people of Badr

[Page 258]

and said to them: Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you." Then Umar's eyes overflowed with tears and he said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." Then the verse was revealed.

As for the explanation of the verse: The address in ﴿O you who have believed﴾ has already been discussed. Likewise, regarding faith (iman), there is the question of whether it is in itself one thing, namely affirmation in the heart, or many things, namely acts of obedience, as the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) have held.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿do not take My enemy and your enemy﴾: the verb ittakhadha (to take) transitively governs two objects, which are "My enemy" and "allies." The word 'aduww (enemy) is of the pattern fa'ul from 'adā (to transgress), like 'afuww (pardoning) from 'afā (to pardon). Because it is of the form of a verbal noun, it is applied to the plural just as it is applied to the singular. Enmity ('adawah) is the opposite of friendship (sadaqah), and the two cannot coexist in one place, at one time, from one aspect, but they may be absent together in the realm of possibility. Al-Zajjaj and al-Karabisi related that "my enemy" means the enemy of my religion. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "A man follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look to whom he takes as a close friend." The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said to Abu Dharr: "O Abu Dharr, which of the bonds of faith is the strongest?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Loyalty for the sake of Allah, love for the sake of Allah, and hatred for the sake of Allah."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿showing them affection﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿showing﴾, with what is it connected? We say: there are several views.

**The first:** The author of al-Nazm (Ibn al-Nazm?) said: it is a description of the indefinite noun, which is "allies." This was stated by al-Farra'.

**The second:** In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it is said: it is permissible for it to be connected to "do not take" as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from its subject (the pronoun), and "allies" is then its adjective.

**The third:** He said: it is also permissible for it to be a new sentence (isti'naf), and then it is not a relative clause qualifying "allies." The preposition bi in "with affection" is like it in His saying: ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation with injustice﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. The meaning is: you convey to them the news and secrets of the Prophet ﷺ with the affection that is between you and them. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿you secretly convey to them with affection﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1].

**The second issue:** There are several discussions concerning the verse.

**The first:** How is it possible to take an enemy as an ally, when enmity is incompatible with love and affection, and love and affection are necessary consequences of that taking? We say: it is not far-fetched that enmity may be in relation to one matter, and love and affection in relation to another. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Our children are the fruit of our hearts."

**The second:** When He said "My enemy," why did He not suffice with it, until He said "and your enemy"? Because the enemy of Allah is only the enemy of the believers. We say: this is a necessary implication of that mutual connection. What does not necessarily follow from being an enemy of the believers is that he is an enemy of Allah, as He said: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you﴾.

**The third:** Why did He say "My enemy and your enemy" and not the reverse? We say: enmity between the believer and the unbeliever is because of the love of Allah, the Exalted, and the love of His Messenger. The love of the servant among the people of faith for the Presence of Allah, the Exalted, is for a cause, whereas the love of the Presence of Allah, the Exalted, for the servant is without cause, because He is absolutely self-sufficient, so He has no need of anything else at all. That which is without cause takes precedence over that which has a cause. Also, when a thing has a relation to two extremes, the higher extreme takes precedence over the lower extreme.

**The fourth:** He said ﴿allies﴾ and did not say "an ally." The enemy and the ally share the same form. We say: just as the definite noun with the definite article covers every individual, so too the definite noun with an annexed noun.

**The fifth:** Some have said the bi (in "with affection") is superfluous. It has already been stated that superfluity is impossible in the Qur'an, and the bi carries a meaning, so it is not superfluous in reality.

[Page 259]

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and you because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have gone out in jihad in My cause and seeking My approval, [would you] secretly convey to them with affection, while I am most knowing of what you conceal and what you declare? And whoever of you does so has certainly strayed from the sound way.﴾

﴿And they have disbelieved﴾: the waw is for the circumstantial clause, meaning: while their state is that they have disbelieved ﴿in what has come to you of the truth﴾, the religion, and it is said: of the Qur'an. ﴿Expelling the Messenger and you﴾, meaning from Makkah to Madinah. ﴿Because you believe﴾, meaning "because you believe" ﴿in Allah, your Lord.﴾ His saying ﴿If you have gone out﴾: al-Zajjaj said: it is a conditional clause whose response precedes it, which is: "do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies." His saying ﴿in jihad in My cause and seeking My approval﴾ are both in the accusative because they are objects of purpose (maf'ulan lahuma). ﴿Secretly convey to them with affection﴾: according to Muqatil, "with the advice." Then He mentioned that nothing of their conditions is hidden from Him, so He said: ﴿while I am most knowing of what you conceal﴾ of affection for the disbelievers ﴿and what you declare﴾, meaning what you make apparent. It is not far-fetched that this is general to everything that is concealed and declared. Some have said: He is most knowing of the inner secrets of the servant, his hidden and his apparent, his outward and inward, his actions and his states. His saying ﴿And whoever of you does so﴾ may refer back to the secret conveying, to the conveying, and to the taking of the disbelievers as allies, since these acts were mentioned earlier. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ has two possible meanings:

**The first:** From Ibn Abbas: he has deviated from the intention of faith in his belief. From Muqatil: he has missed the aim of the path to guidance.

Then there are discussions concerning the verse:

**The first:** ﴿If you have gone out﴾ is connected to "do not take." That is, do not befriend My enemies if you are My allies. ﴿Secretly convey﴾ is a new sentence, meaning: what benefit is there for you in your secrecy, when you know that concealment and declaration are alike in My knowledge?

**The second:** Someone may say: ﴿If you have gone out﴾ and the rest of the verse is a conditional proposition. If that is so, then the condition, which is "if you have gone out," cannot exist without that prohibition, and it is known that it can exist. We say: this whole is a condition for what the prohibition requires, not for the prohibition by its explicit wording. The whole cannot exist without that, because that is always present. The benefit in "seeking My approval" is clear, since going out may be in seeking Allah's approval and may not be.

**The third:** He, the Exalted, said ﴿what you conceal and what you declare﴾ and did not say "what you kept secret and what you declared," even though "kept secret" would better fit what preceded it, which is "you secretly convey." We say: there is more emphasis in "conceal" than in that, for concealment is more intense than secrecy. This is shown by His saying: ﴿He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾ [Ta-Ha: 7], meaning: what is more hidden than the secret.

**The fourth:** He said ﴿what you conceal﴾ and placed the knowledge of concealment before the declaration, even though the former necessarily implies the latter but not vice versa. We say: this is in relation to our knowledge, not in relation to His knowledge, the Exalted, for the two are alike in His knowledge, as already stated. Also, the aim is to show what is most hidden, which is disbelief, so it is placed first.

**The fifth:** He, the Exalted, said ﴿And whoever of you does so﴾. What is the benefit of His saying ﴿of you﴾, when it is known that whoever does this act ﴿has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾? We say: if by ﴿of you﴾ is meant "of the believers," then the benefit is clear, because whoever does that act does not necessarily have to be a believer.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 60, verses 2–3:

Page 260
Then He informed the believers of the enmity of the disbelievers of Makkah, saying:
﴿If they gain the upper hand over you, they will be your enemies and will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection. He will distinguish between you, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿Yathqafuukum﴾ means they will overcome you and gain power over you. ﴿Yakununu lakum﴾ means they will be in the utmost enmity, and this is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: they will prevail over you, or they will be friendly with you. ﴿And they will stretch out their hands﴾ with beating, ﴿and their tongues﴾ with insults. ﴿And they wish﴾ that you would return to their religion. The meaning is that the enemies of Allah do not sincerely love the allies of Allah, because of the opposition between them. ﴿Your relatives will not benefit you﴾: when Hatib was rebuked for what he had done, he excused himself by saying that he had relatives there, namely kinsfolk, and children among them, and that he had no one there to protect his clan. So he wanted to create a favor with them so that they would treat kindly those of his clan he had left behind in Makkah. Thus Allah said: ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you﴾, those for whose sake you befriend the disbelievers and draw near to them out of fear for them. Then He said: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will distinguish between you﴾, and between your relatives and your children, so the people of faith will enter Paradise and the people of disbelief will enter the Fire. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, that is, of what Hatib did. Then in the verse there are several discussions:

The first: what the author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿If they gain the upper hand over you, they will be your enemies﴾ — how does it bring the answer of the conditional in the present tense like it, then say ﴿and they wish﴾ in the past tense? We say: although the past tense in the conditional construction functions like the present tense in grammatical terms, there is in it a subtle point, as if it were said: they wished, before everything, your disbelief and apostasy.

The second: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a time adverb for what? We say: for His saying ﴿will not benefit you﴾, or it may be a time adverb for ﴿will distinguish﴾. Ibn Kathir read yufsalu with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the sad, and yafsilu with the verb in the active form, whose subject is Allah, and nafsilu with the nun.

The third: He, exalted is He, said ﴿and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ and did not say "Knowing (khabir)", although khabir is more emphatic in knowledge of a thing. The answer: khabir is more emphatic in knowledge, but basir is more manifest in it, because it makes their deeds like something perceived by the sense of sight. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 60, verse 4:

Then Allah, exalted is He, said:

﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of whatever you worship other than Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone," except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have no power to do anything for you against Allah. Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the final return."﴾

Know that al-Uswa (the example) is that which one takes as a model, like al-Qudwa (the pattern) for that which is followed. It is said: "He is your uswa," meaning you are like him and he is like you. The plural of al-Uswa is Usan. So al-Uswa is a name for everything that is followed as a model. The exegetes said: Allah, exalted is He, informed that Abraham and his companions disassociated themselves from their people and opposed them, and said to them: "Indeed, we are free of you." And He commanded the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to take them as an example, both in their deeds and in their words. Al-Farra' said: It means, "Have you not followed the example of Abraham, O Hatib, in disowning his family, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when they said to their people, 'Indeed, we are free of you'﴾ and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father, 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you'﴾, while he was a polytheist." Mujahid said: They were forbidden to take as an example Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father, so that they would not ask forgiveness for the polytheists. Mujahid and Qatadah said: Follow the whole command of Abraham except his asking forgiveness for his father. It was also said: Disown the disbelievers of your people, for you have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him among the believers in disowning their people, but not in asking forgiveness for his father. Ibn Qutaybah said: He means that Abraham opposed and forsook them in everything except his saying to his father: (I will surely ask forgiveness for you). Ibn al-Anbari said: The matter is not as he stated; rather, the meaning is: "There has certainly been for you an example in everything he did, except his saying to his father: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿but I have no power to do anything for you against Allah﴾ is part of Abraham's speech to his father; he says to him: "I cannot avail you anything, nor can I ward off the punishment of Allah from you if you associate partners with Him." So he promised him forgiveness in hope of his becoming Muslim. Ibn Abbas said: Among the supplications of Abraham and his companions was: ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied﴾, and so on to the end of the verse, meaning, in all our affairs. ﴿And to You we have turned in repentance﴾: we have returned to You in repentance from disobedience, for the final return is only to Your presence.

In the verse there are several discussions:

The first: One may ask: ﴿until you believe in Allah alone﴾, what is the benefit of His saying ﴿alone﴾, since belief in Him together with others is among the necessary implications, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each believes in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]? We reply: Belief in the angels, the books, the messengers and the Last Day is among the necessary implications of believing in Allah alone, since what is meant by His saying "alone" is alone in divinity (uluhiyya). We have no doubt that believing in the divinity of other than Him is not belief in Allah, for in reality it is associating partners with Him, and the polytheist is not a believer.

The second: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except for the saying of Abraham﴾ is an exception from what? We say: from His saying ﴿an excellent example﴾, because by "the excellent example" He meant their saying which they were obliged to follow, and to take as a sunnah by which they would be guided.

The third: If His saying ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ is excepted from the statement that preceded it, namely ﴿an excellent example﴾, then what about His saying ﴿but I have no power to do anything for you against Allah﴾, which is not fit to be excepted? Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Who then has any power for you against Allah in anything?"﴾? We reply: Allah, exalted is He, intended to except the whole of his saying to his father, and the intention to promise forgiveness for him and what follows it is built upon it and subordinate to it, as if He had said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and my capacity is only to ask forgiveness."

The fourth: If it is asked: with what is His saying ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied﴾ connected? We reply: with what precedes the exception, and it is part of the excellent example. It is also possible that the meaning is the command to say this statement, as instruction for the believers and as completion of what He enjoined on them of severing ties between them and the disbelievers, and of following Abraham and his people in disowning them, as an alert to turning to the presence of Allah, exalted is He, and seeking refuge in Him.

The fifth: If it is asked: what is the benefit of this order? We reply: It contains benefits that none but Him encompasses. The apparent meaning of that sentence is to say: reliance (tawakkul) is for the sake of benefit, and the benefit of reliance depends on taqwa. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. Taqwa is repentance (inabah), since taqwa is guarding against what is not fitting among matters, and the indication that the return and the final destination of all creatures is His sacred presence alone. So it is as if He mentioned the thing, and mentioned after it what is among its necessary implications, to convey that benefit as it should be.

The readings of "bura'u" are in four forms: bura'u like shuraka'u (partners); bira'un like zuraf (plural of zarif); buraʾu with the damma replacing the kasra, like rukhal; and bara'un described by the verbal noun. And al-barāʾ and al-barāʾah, like al-ṭamāʾ and al-ṭamāʾah.

Then God, exalted is He, said: "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise." "There has certainly been for you in them an excellent pattern for whoever hopes in God and the Last Day. And whoever turns away—indeed, God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy." "Perhaps God will place affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity. And God is competent, and God is Forgiving and Merciful."

His saying, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve," is part of the supplication of Ibrahim (Abraham). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not give our enemies power over us, lest they think that they are upon the truth." Mujahid said: "Do not punish us at their hands, nor with a punishment from You, lest they say, 'If these were upon the truth, that would not have befallen them.'" It was also said: "Do not extend provision to them without us, for that is a trial for them." It was also said: His saying "do not make us a trial" means a punishment, that is, a cause by which the disbelievers are punished; and according to this view, the verse is not part of the words of Ibrahim.

His exalted saying, "Our Lord, and forgive us," and the verse that follows, are part of what has passed, as if it were said to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ): "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve." Then He repeated the mention of the pattern for the sake of emphasis in the speech, saying: "There has certainly been for you in them an excellent pattern," that is, in Ibrahim and those with him. This is the exhortation to take Ibrahim and his people as a model. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They used to hate whoever opposed God and love whoever God loves."

His exalted saying, "for whoever hopes in God," is a substitute (badal) for His saying "for you" (lakum), and it is a clarification that this pattern is for whoever fears God and fears the punishment of the Hereafter. "And whoever turns away" means he turns away from following their example and inclines toward the affection of the disbelievers. "Indeed, God is the Free of need" from opposing His enemies, "the Praiseworthy" toward His friends.

As for His saying, "Perhaps God (ʿasā Allāh)": Muqatil said: When God commanded the believers to be hostile to the disbelievers, they became severe in their enmity toward their fathers, their sons, and all their relatives, and in disavowing them. So God, exalted is He, sent down His saying: "Perhaps God will place between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity" — that is, among the disbelievers of Makkah — "affection," and that is by their inclination toward Islam, their mixing with the people of Islam, and their intermarriage with them. It was also said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) married Umm Habibah, and the stubbornness of Abu Sufyan softened at that, and his resolve in enmity relaxed. Umm Habibah had embraced Islam and had emigrated with her husband 'Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh to Abyssinia. He became a Christian and tried to turn her to Christianity, but she refused and remained steadfast in her religion. Her husband died, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent to the Negus, who proposed to her on his behalf, and he paid on his behalf to her four hundred dinars. When this reached her father, he said: "That stallion's nose will not be rubbed in the dust." The phrase "perhaps" (ʿasā) is a promise from God, the Exalted: "and between those among them with whom you have been at enmity, affection," meaning a group of the Quraysh who believed after the conquest of Makkah, among them Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and Hakim ibn Hizam. God, exalted is He, is capable of turning hearts, changing conditions, and facilitating the causes of affection. "And God is Forgiving and Merciful" toward them when they repent, embrace Islam, and return to the presence of God, exalted is He. Some of them said: Do not abandon one another completely, for God is aware of what is hidden and of inner secrets. And it is narrated: "Love your beloved moderately, for perhaps he may one day become your hater, and hate your hater moderately, for perhaps he may one day become your beloved."

Among the investigations into this wisdom: His exalted saying, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial," if its interpretation is, for example, "do not give our enemies power over us," why did He leave this and instead say that? We say: when the wording is such that it may be a expression for this, then when He states it, it is as if He stated this and that together, and in it are benefits not present in limiting it to one of those interpretations.

Second: One may ask: what is the benefit of His saying, "and forgive us, our Lord," when the statement would have been complete if it were said: "do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve; indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise"? We say: they sought freedom from being a trial, and freedom from being a trial cannot exist without forgiveness, for if the sinner were not forgiven, he would be subdued by the subjugation of punishment, and that is a trial, since trial is an expression of being subdued. And "the Praiseworthy" (al-Hamid) may mean the one who praises, and it may mean the one who is praised. The Praiseworthy is one who deserves praise from His creation for the blessings He has bestowed upon them; the one who praises is one who praises the creation and thanks them, when He rewards them with abundant reward for little deeds.

Then, after mentioning the prohibition of the believers' complete severance from the disbelievers, He granted a concession regarding maintaining ties with those disbelievers who had not fought them, saying:

Then God, exalted is He, said: "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise." "There has certainly been for you in them an excellent pattern for whoever hopes in God and the Last Day. And whoever turns away—indeed, God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy." "Perhaps God will place affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity. And God is competent, and God is Forgiving and Merciful."

His saying, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve," is part of the supplication of Ibrahim (Abraham). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not give our enemies power over us, lest they think that they are upon the truth." Mujahid said: "Do not punish us at their hands, nor with a punishment from You, lest they say, 'If these were upon the truth, that would not have befallen them.'" It was also said: "Do not extend provision to them without us, for that is a trial for them." It was also said: His saying "do not make us a trial" means a punishment, that is, a cause by which the disbelievers are punished; and according to this view, the verse is not part of the words of Ibrahim.

His exalted saying, "Our Lord, and forgive us," and the verse that follows, are part of what has passed, as if it were said to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ): "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve." Then He repeated the mention of the pattern for the sake of emphasis in the speech, saying: "There has certainly been for you in them an excellent pattern," that is, in Ibrahim and those with him. This is the exhortation to take Ibrahim and his people as a model. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They used to hate whoever opposed God and love whoever God loves."

"And whoever turns away" means he turns away from following their example and inclines toward the affection of the disbelievers. "Indeed, God is the Free of need" from opposing His enemies, "the Praiseworthy" toward His friends.

As for His saying, "Perhaps God (ʿasā Allāh)": Muqatil said: When God commanded the believers to be hostile to the disbelievers, they became severe in their enmity toward their fathers, their sons, and all their relatives, and in disavowing them. So God, exalted is He, sent down His saying: "Perhaps God will place between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity" — that is, among the disbelievers of Makkah — "affection," and that is by their inclination toward Islam, their mixing with the people of Islam, and their intermarriage with them. It was also said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) married Umm Habibah, and the stubbornness of Abu Sufyan softened at that, and his resolve in enmity relaxed. Umm Habibah had embraced Islam and had emigrated with her husband 'Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh to Abyssinia. He became a Christian and tried to turn her to Christianity, but she refused and remained steadfast in her religion. Her husband died, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent to the Negus, who proposed to her on his behalf, and he paid on his behalf to her four hundred dinars. When this reached her father, he said: "That stallion's nose will not be rubbed in the dust." The phrase "perhaps" (ʿasā) is a promise from God, the Exalted: "and between those among them with whom you have been at enmity, affection," meaning a group of the Quraysh who believed after the conquest of Makkah, among them Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and Hakim ibn Hizam. God, exalted is He, is capable of turning hearts, changing conditions, and facilitating the causes of affection. "And God is Forgiving and Merciful" toward them when they repent, embrace Islam, and return to the presence of God, exalted is He. Some of them said: Do not abandon one another completely, for God is aware of what is hidden and of inner secrets. And it is narrated: "Love your beloved moderately, for perhaps he may one day become your hater, and hate your hater moderately, for perhaps he may one day become your beloved."

We say: when the wording is such that it may be a expression for this, then when He states it, it is as if He stated this and that together, and in it are benefits not present in limiting it to one of those interpretations.

Then, after mentioning the prohibition of the believers' complete severance from the disbelievers, He granted a concession regarding maintaining ties with those disbelievers who had not fought them, saying:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 60, verses 8–9:

﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over the religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being kind to them and dealing justly with them. Indeed, Allah loves those who deal justly.﴾ ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over the religion, expel you from your homes, and back up [others] in your expulsion—from allying with them. And whoever allies with them, it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

The scholars differed over the meaning of ﴿those who do not fight you﴾. Most of them hold that they are the people of the covenant (ahl al-'ahd) who made a pact with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to abandon fighting and to refrain from aiding enmity against him, and they were Khuza'ah. They had pledged to the Messenger that they would not fight him or expel him, so the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to show kindness and fulfil [the pact] until the end of their term. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: they are those who believed in Makkah but did not emigrate. It was also said: they are the women and children. And it is reported from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed concerning Asma' bint Abi Bakr, whose mother Qutaylah came to her while she was a polytheist, bringing gifts; she did not accept them and did not permit her to enter, so the Prophet ﷺ commanded her to let her enter, to accept from her, to honour her and to treat her well. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they were a people from Banu Hashim, among them al-'Abbas, who were taken out [to Badr] against their will. And it is reported from al-Hasan that the Muslims asked the Messenger of Allah for permission regarding their relatives among the polytheists, that they might maintain ties with them, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. It was also said that the verse concerns the polytheists in general. Qatadah said it was abrogated by the verse of fighting.

His saying ﴿that you be kind to them﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿those who do not fight you﴾, and likewise ﴿that you ally with them﴾ is a substitution for ﴿those who fight you﴾. The meaning is: He does not forbid you from showing kindness to these people; rather, He forbids you only from allying with those people. This is a mercy towards them, given the severity of their enmity. The commentators said: this verse indicates the permissibility of goodness between polytheists and Muslims, even though close allegiance (al-muwalah) is cut off.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and deal justly with them﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said it means by maintaining ties and otherwise. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who deal justly﴾: he means the people of goodness and kinship. Muqatil said: [it means] that you fulfil their covenant to them and act equitably.

Then he mentioned who those are that He forbids them from maintaining ties with, saying: ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over the religion﴾ ﴿—from allying with them.﴾ And in this there is a subtle point: it emphasises His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 60, verse 10:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, test them. Allah knows best their faith. Then if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them. And give the disbelievers what they have spent. And there is no blame upon you in marrying them when you have given them their compensation. And do not hold on to marriage ties with disbelieving women. Ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

In the arrangement (nazm) of these verses there is a good and reasonable aspect. The hostile person is in one of three states: either his hostility continues, or it is hoped that he will abandon hostility, or he abandons hostility and submits. Allah, exalted is He, has explained their states in these verses and commanded the Muslims to deal with them in each state according to what the state requires.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4], it refers to the first state. Then His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will place affection between you and those of them with whom you have enmity﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 7], refers to the second state. Then His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you﴾, refers to the third state. Then in it there is a subtle point, an admonition, and an exhortation to noble character, because He, exalted is He, did not command the believers, in response to those three states, with recompense except with that which is best, and with speech except with that which is most fitting.

Know that He, exalted is He, named them "believers" because of the emergence from them of what requires faith, which is the statement of testimony (kalimat al-shahadah), and nothing appeared from them that contradicts it. Or it is because they are approaching the firm establishment of their faith through the testing (imtihan), which is trial by oath. The oath is for the sake of the prevailing assumption (ghalabat al-zann) of their faith. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say to the woman being tested: 'By Allah, besides whom there is no god, did you not leave out of hatred for a husband? By Allah, did you not leave out of desire for a land from land to land? By Allah, did you not leave out seeking worldly gain? By Allah, you did not leave except out of love for Allah and His Messenger.'"

His saying, ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾, means: Allah, not you, knows their faith, and Allah alone governs the hidden matters. ﴿Then if you know them﴾, means the knowledge which is an expression for the prevailing assumption through the oath and other means. ﴿Then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾, meaning, do not send them back to their polytheist husbands. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾, and ﴿Give them what they have spent﴾, means: give their husbands the like of what they paid to them as dowries. This was because the treaty at the year of al-Hudaybiyyah was that whoever came to you from the people of Makkah would be returned to them, and whoever came to Makkah from among you would not be returned to you. They wrote that agreement as a document and sealed it. Then Subay'ah bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyyah came, a Muslim woman, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was at al-Hudaybiyyah. Her husband, Musafir al-Makhzumi, approached (and it was said: Sayfi ibn al-Rahib) and said: "O Muhammad, return my wife to me, for you have stipulated for us a condition: that you would return to us whoever comes to you from us, and this is the ink of the document, which has not yet dried." So it was revealed as clarification, because the condition was made only for men, not for women. "It is related from al-Zuhri that he said: Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it came, and she was a young woman (ʿatiq), and her family came seeking from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he return her to them. She had fled from her husband Amr ibn al-As, and with her were her two brothers, Umarah and al-Walid. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her two brothers and held her back. They said: 'Return her to us.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'The condition was for men, not for women.'" And from al-Dahhak: "The covenant was that if a woman comes to you from us who is not upon your religion, you return her to us; and if she enters your religion while she has a husband, she is returned to her husband who spent upon her. The Prophet (ﷺ) had a similar condition. Then this ruling and this covenant were abrogated (nusikha), and the Messenger, peace be upon him, made her swear, so she swore, and he gave her husband what he had spent. Then Umar married her."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there is no blame upon you in marrying them when you have given them their compensation﴾, means their dowries, since the dowry is the compensation for intimacy (ujr al-bud'). ﴿And do not hold on to marriage ties with disbelieving women﴾. The ʿișma is that by which one holds fast, through a covenant or otherwise. There is no ʿișma between you and them, nor the bond of marriage in the same way. It is related from Ibn Abbas that the difference of the two abodes (ikhtilaf al-darayn) severs the bond. It was also said: "Do not sit with the disbelieving women." It was read as "tumsikū" with light and heavy pronunciation, and "tumsikū" means "do not hold on to." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Ask for what you have spent﴾, is that if a woman from among you joins the people of the covenant among the disbelievers as an apostate, then ask them for what you have spent of the dowry if they withhold it and do not give it to you; then they are obligated to pay her dowry just as it is paid to them. This is His saying, ﴿and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾, meaning between the Muslims and the disbelievers.

There are discussions regarding the verse:

The first: His saying, ﴿Then test them﴾, is a command in the sense of obligation, or in the sense of recommendation, or in some other sense. Al-Wahidi said: it is in the sense of desirability (istihbab).

The second: What is the benefit of His saying, ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾, when that is known without doubt? We say: its benefit is to make clear that there is no way to what the soul is reassured by, namely full comprehension of the reality of their faith, for that is among the matters reserved to the Knower of the unseen.

The third: What is the benefit of His saying, ﴿nor are they lawful for them﴾? It might be possible that it refers to one side only, not the other. We say: this is by consideration of faith on the part of both them and them, since faith on both sides is a condition for lawfulness; and because mention from both sides emphasizes the removal of lawfulness, and this carries a benefit not found otherwise. If it is said: Grant that it is so, but His saying, ﴿So do not return them to the disbelievers﴾ suffices, since neither of them is lawful for the other, so there is no need for additional wording, and that is the intended meaning and nothing more. We say: uttering this wording does not convey the removal of lawfulness from both sides in the way that uttering that wording does, and this is evident.

The fourth discussion: How did He call the assumption "knowledge" in His saying, ﴿Then if you know them﴾? We say: it is of the category that the prevailing assumption and what ijtihad leads to, and analogy (qiyas), take the place of knowledge, and that its holder is not included in His saying, ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra: 36].

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if any of your wives have gone over to the disbelievers, and you then have a victory (fa-'aqabtum), give to those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.ﴩ

It is related from al-Zuhri and Masruq that among the judgments of Allah the Exalted is that the Muslims should demand from the disbelievers the dower (mahr) of a Muslim woman when she has come over to them, and the disbelievers should demand from the Muslims the dower of those of their women who have become Muslims and come to us. The Muslims accepted the judgment of Allah, but the polytheists refused, so this was revealed: ﴿And if any of your wives have gone (fata)﴾, meaning: they got ahead of you and escaped from you.

al-Hasan and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Umm Hakim bint Abi Sufyan, who apostatized and left her husband 'Abbas ibn Tamim al-Qurashi, and no woman other than Quraysh women apostatized except her. Then she returned to Islam.

His saying ﴿fa-'aqabtum﴾ means "then you gained booty (fa-ghanimtum)," according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq and Muqatil. Abu 'Ubayda said: "You obtained an 'uqba from them," meaning a turn of victory. Al-Mubarrad said: ﴿fa-'aqabtum﴾ means "you did to them what had been done to you," i.e., you were victorious. It derives from your saying: "al-'uqba is for so-and-so," meaning the outcome (al-'aqiba). The interpretation of al-'aqiba is "the final turn (al-karra al-akhira)." The meaning of 'aqabtum is: you raided, being those who take turns, raid after raid. It was also said: the turn and the victory were yours, so give the wives' husbands from the top of the spoils what they had spent on them as dower, and this is His saying: ﴿give to those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent﴾. It is also read: fa-a'qabtum, and fa-'aqqabtum with shadda, and fa-'aqabtum without shadda, with the qaf vowelled either with fatha or kasra.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 60, verse 12:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children, nor bring a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

It is narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ finished, on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, taking the pledge from the men, he began taking the pledge from the women while he was on al-Safa, and ʿUmar was below him, taking the pledge from the women by the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and conveying it from him. Hind bint ʿUtbah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, was veiled and disguised, fearing that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would recognize her. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I take your pledge that you will not associate anything with Allah." Hind raised her head and said: "By Allah, we used to worship idols, and you are demanding of us a thing that we have not seen you demand of men. You take the pledge of men only for Islam and jihad." He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "And that you will not steal." Hind said: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man, and I have taken some of his wealth, a small amount, and I do not know whether it is lawful for me or not." Abu Sufyan said: "Whatever you have taken of anything in the past and in the future, it is lawful for you." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and recognized her, and said to her: "Are you indeed Hind bint ʿUtbah?" She said: "Yes, so pardon what has passed, O Prophet of Allah; may Allah pardon you." He said: "And that you will not commit adultery." She said: "Does a free woman commit adultery?" In another narration: "Not one of them has ever committed adultery." He said: "And that you will not kill your children." She said: "We raised them when they were small, and you killed them when they were grown; you and they know best." Her son Handhalah ibn Abi Sufyan had been killed on the day of Badr. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, laughed until he fell back, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled. He said: "And that you will not bring a slander you have invented." That is, that she falsely attributes to her husband what is not from him. Hind said: "By Allah, slander is indeed an ugly thing, and you only command us to what is right and to noble character." He said: "And that you will not disobey me in what is right." She said: "By Allah, we did not sit in this gathering of ours with the intention of disobeying you in anything."

As for His saying ﴿and do not steal﴾, it includes the prohibition of betrayal in wealth and of shortcoming in worship, for it is said: "The worst thief is the one who steals from his prayer."

His saying ﴿and do not commit adultery﴾ may include the reality of adultery and its precursors too, in accordance with what the Prophet ﷺ said: "The two hands commit adultery, the two eyes commit adultery, the two feet commit adultery, and the private part makes it true or false."

His saying ﴿and do not kill their children﴾ intended the burying of daughters alive, which the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to do. Then it is general in every kind of killing of children and others.

His saying ﴿and do not bring a slander﴾ forbids backbiting, meaning that none of them should speak ill of her companion, which would result in severance. It may also be a prohibition against attributing a child to other than their husbands. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "She should not attribute to her husband a child that is not his." Al-Farraʾ (a grammarian and exegete) said: "A woman would pick up a newborn and say to her husband: 'This is my child from you.' That is the slander invented between their hands and feet, because when the mother gives birth, the child falls between her hands and feet." The meaning is not a prohibition against adultery, since the prohibition against adultery has already been mentioned.

His saying ﴿nor disobey you in what is right﴾ means every matter that agrees with the obedience of Allah. It is also said: "In a matter of righteousness and piety." It is also said: "In every matter that contains good judgment," meaning: they should not disobey you in all your commands. Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Kalbi and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: ﴿nor disobey you in what is right﴾ means in what you command them and forbid them from, such as wailing, tearing clothes, cutting or plucking hair, tearing the collar, scratching the face, speaking to men unless it is with a close unmarriageable relative (dhu rahim mahram), being alone with a man who is not a mahram, or travelling except with a mahram. Some of them restricted this "right" to wailing. From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Four things from the matters of the Jahiliyyah will remain in my nation and they will not abandon them: boasting about lineage, insulting ancestry, seeking rain by the stars, and wailing." He also said: "The wailing woman, if she does not repent before her death, will be raised on the Day of Resurrection wearing a garment of tar and a shirt of scabies." And he ﷺ said: "He is not one of us who strikes his cheeks, tears his collar, and calls out with the call of the Jahiliyyah."

His saying ﴿then accept their pledge﴾ is the answer to ﴿when﴾ (idha). That is: when they pledge to you on these conditions, then accept their pledge. The scholars differed over the manner of the pledge. They said: he would take their pledge while there was a cloth between their hands. It is also said: he would stipulate the pledge to them while ʿUmar shook their hands, as al-Kalbi said. It is also said: it was by speech. It is also said: he called for a vessel of water, dipped his hand into it, and then they dipped their hands into it. The hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ never touched the hand of a woman.

There are several discussions concerning the verse:

The first discussion: Allah the Exalted said ﴿when believing women come to you﴾ and did not say "then test them," as He said regarding the emigrant women (in the verse before this).

The answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: the testing is accomplished by His saying ﴿that they will not associate﴾ up to the end of it.

The second: the emigrant women came from the Abode of War, so they had no knowledge of the laws of Islam, and therefore testing was necessary. As for the believing women, they were in the Abode of Islam and knew the laws, so there was no need for testing.

The second: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿between their hands and their feet﴾, and what is its meaning? We say: whoever says that when a woman picks up a child, she picks it up with her hand and walks to take it with her foot. So when she attributes it to her husband, she has brought a slander she has invented between her hands and her feet. It is also said: they invent it against themselves, when they say: "This is our child," and it is not so, since the child is the child of fornication. It is also said: when the mother gives birth to the child, it falls between her hands and feet.

The third: What is the reason for the order of the things mentioned and the placing of some of them before others in the verse? We say: He placed first the most ugly of them, then what is next in ugliness, and so on to the end. It is also said: He placed first among the things mentioned what is most apparent among them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 60, verse 13:

Page 268

Then the Exalted said:
﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry; they have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves.﴾

Ibn ‘Abbas said: He means Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. The verse means: do not take the Jews and the polytheists as allies. This is because a group of poor Muslims used to inform the Jews of the news of the Muslims, due to their need for them, so they were forbidden from this. "They have despaired of the Hereafter" means that the Jews denied Muhammad (ﷺ) while they knew that he was the Messenger of Allah, and that they had ruined their Hereafter by their denial of him. "They have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves": the restriction by this qualifier is evident, because when they die in their disbelief, the knowledge of their abandonment and their lack of portion in the Hereafter is certain. This is the view of al-Kalbi and a group, meaning: the disbelievers who have died have despaired of Paradise and of there being any good for them in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan said: it means the living disbelievers have despaired of the dead. Abu Ishaq said: the Jews who opposed the Prophet (ﷺ) have despaired, just as the disbelievers who do not believe in resurrection have despaired of their dead.

And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
